query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal annealing treatment designed to induce interfacial complexion formation at the lamellar boundaries of the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will mitigate dislocation pile‐ups, thereby reducing local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation. This modification is expected to significantly enhance room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even moderately increasing the high inherent strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies that currently exhibits high strength but limited room-temperature ductility due to dislocation pile‐ups at internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted thermal treatment with parameters (temperature and time) optimized to trigger atomic segregation at the lamellar interfaces, thereby forming ultrathin, ductile intergranular films (complexions).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under standard strain rate conditions, ensuring that any improvements in ductility and strength are relevant to ambient service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrathin, ductile intergranular films (i.e., interfacial complexions) that form at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The induced complexion reduces the impedance to dislocation motion through the lamellar interfaces. This promotes smoother dislocation transmission, prevents dislocation accumulation and local stress concentration, and delays microcrack nucleation, thereby overcoming the brittleness issue while preserving (or enhancing) the alloy’s intrinsic strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature tensile ductility (i.e., higher elongation at failure) with maintained or slightly increased yield strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy, which exhibits high strength but suffers from limited tensile ductility at room temperature due to dislocation pile-ups and associated microcracking at the phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under room-temperature mechanical loading. Excessive thermal treatment (e.g., too high temperature or too long duration) might lead to unintended phase changes or coarsening that could compromise strength, so the treatment window is critical.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in ductility and strength is uncertain and will depend on optimizing the thermal treatment parameters. Additionally, the stability and uniformity of the interfacial complexions under varied service conditions need further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of alloy samples from the same baseline eutectic high-entropy material. Subject these samples to the proposed controlled thermal treatment under various parameter sets (different temperatures and times) to induce interfacial complexion formation. Use a control group of untreated samples. Characterize the microstructure using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to detect the presence of ultrathin intergranular films at lamellar interfaces and to observe dislocation activity during in situ tensile tests. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture.
measurements: HRTEM imaging of lamellar boundaries to confirm the formation of interfacial complexions
In situ tensile test observations of dislocation behavior at interfaces
Room-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, percent elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal treatment does not lead to the formation of detectable interfacial complexions at the lamellar boundaries or if the treated samples do not exhibit any statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (and/or show a reduction in strength) compared to untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual‐phase lamellar colonies in its as‐processed state.
frame.goal: Achieve a significant improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility (i.e., reduce brittleness) while maintaining or enhancing the high strength inherent to the starting material.
frame.limitation: The current alloy shows limited room-temperature ductility due to the susceptibility to dislocation pile‐ups at internal (lamellar) boundaries, which lead to local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure during strain.
constraints: intervention should overcome or mitigate the dislocation pile‐up mechanism at internal boundaries
must retain or increase the alloy's strength relative to the untreated state
should address performance at room-temperature tensile conditions
frame.regime: Room-temperature tensile testing and operating conditions, where the alloy is subjected to standard strain rates to evaluate both strength and ductility.
prior_attempts: Previous studies on similar dual-phase or eutectic high-entropy alloys have focused on microstructural modifications (e.g., heat treatments or minor alloying adjustments) to refine colony size or adjust phase fractions. However, these methods fell short in directly mitigating the dislocation accumulation at phase boundaries without sacrificing strength.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) on eutectic high-entropy alloys established that a dual‐phase lamellar microstructure can yield high strength and moderate ductility; however, the intrinsic internal interfaces served as sites for dislocation pile-ups. Later studies (e.g., PMC10213035) used stepwise thermo‐mechanical processes to induce coherent precipitation and tailored interfacial structures, which improved yield strength and ductility by partially modulating dislocation behavior. Yet, none of these efforts directly resolved the dislocation accumulation at the lamellar colony boundaries that creates local stress concentrations and microcracking.
decision.unsolved: A direct strategy to modify the intrinsic nature of the lamellar interfaces—so that dislocation pile‐ups are mitigated without sacrificing the high inherent strength—remains unsolved.
decision.lever: controlled thermal treatment to induce interfacial complexion formation at the lamellar boundaries
decision.why: Building on the trend where conventional microstructure refinement and precipitate engineering improved overall performance but left the dislocation pile‐up issue unaddressed, a targeted thermal treatment can trigger beneficial atomic segregation at the internal interfaces. This complexion engineering would create ultrathin, ductile intergranular films that facilitate smoother dislocation transmission, reduce local stress concentration and microcracking, and thus overcome the brittleness while retaining or enhancing the alloy’s strength under room-temperature tensile conditions.
